**Sūrat Īlāf Quraysh (Surah 106), Makkī, and it has four verses.**

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿For the covenant (ītlāf) of the Quraysh,﴾ ﴿their covenant of the caravan of winter and summer,﴾ ﴿let them worship the Lord of this House,﴾ ﴿who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear.﴾

*Quraysh* is a proper name for a tribe. They are the Banū al-Naḍr ibn Kinānah, so whoever descends from the Banū al-Naḍr is a Qurashī, but not the Banū Kinānah. It is also said that they are the Banū Fihr ibn Mālik ibn al-Naḍr, so whoever was not born of Fihr is not a Qurashī. Al-Qurṭubī said: The first opinion is more sound and more established. They were named this because they gathered together after being scattered. *Taqrīsh* means gathering and joining together, and from it is the verse of the poet:

*"Brothers who gathered the sins (al-dhunūb) against us, in a tale of their age and their antiquity."*

They had been scattered outside the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram), and Quṣayy ibn Kilāb gathered them within the Ḥaram until they took it as their dwelling. From this is his saying:

*"Our father Quṣayy was called the Gatherer (mujammi'), by him God gathered the tribes from Fihr."*

Al-Farrā' said: *Taqarrush* means earning a livelihood. One says *qarasha yaqrishu qarshan*, meaning he earned and gathered, and from this Quraysh was named. It is also said that they used to search out the one in need among the pilgrims (ḥājj) to meet his needs, and *al-qarsh* means searching. From this is the verse of the poet:

*"O speaker who searches among us at the presence of ʿAmr, and is there any survival for that?"*

Mu'āwiya asked Ibn ʿAbbās: Why was Quraysh named Quraysh? He said: After a creature in the sea, the strongest of its beasts, called *al-qirsh*, which eats and is not eaten, and which overcomes and is not overcome. From this is the saying of Tubba':

*"Quraysh are those who dwell in the sea, by them Quraysh was named Quraysh.*
*It eats the lean and the fat, and leaves none of its feathers to one with two wings.*
*Thus in the lands is the tribe of Quraysh, eating up the lands with a sparse eating.*
*And for them at the end of time there will be a prophet, who will make much slaughter among them and inflict wounds."*

In the *Kashshāf* (of al-Zamakhsharī): It is a beast that plays with ships and cannot be subdued except by fire. If Quraysh is derived from a triliteral with an added letter, then it is a diminutive by truncation (*tarkhīm*); if it is from a bare triliteral root, then it is a diminutive on the original form of diminution.

*Al-shitāʾ* (winter) and *al-ṣayf* (summer) are two well-known seasons of the four seasons of the year. The hamza of *al-shitāʾ* is substituted from a waw. They said *shatā yashtū*, and *shatwatan*. *Al-shitāʾ* is a singular noun and is not the plural of *shatwa*.

﴿For the covenant of Quraysh,﴾ ﴿their covenant of the caravan of winter and summer,﴾ ﴿let them worship the Lord of this House,﴾ ﴿who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear.﴾

This sūrah is Makkī according to the majority, and Madanī according to al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Ibn al-Sāʾib. Its connection to what precedes it is evident, especially if the *lām* is taken as related to the verb *faʿalanā* (we did that), in the sense of *"for the covenant of Quraysh"* – the view of al-Akhfash – or by implying *faʿalnā dhālika li-ītlāf Quraysh* (We did that for the covenant of Quraysh), which is reported from al-Akhfash as well: *"until they settle in their land."* So He mentioned this as a favour upon them, for had the People of the Elephant been given power over them, they would have been dispersed across the lands and regions, and their word would not have been united. Al-Zamakhsharī said: This is like *tadmīn* in poetry (*tadmīn*: the sense of a line depending on the one before it in a way that cannot be correct without it). In Ubayy's codex (muṣḥaf), the two (sūrahs) are one single sūrah without separation. It is reported from ʿUmar that he recited them in the second rakʿah of the Maghrib prayer, and in the first he recited *al-Tīn*. The meaning is that He destroyed the people of Abyssinia who had intended them, so that people would hear of this, and would stand in greater awe of them, and would show them exceeding reverence, until security was organized for them in their journey. End.

Al-Ḥawfī said: A group rejected this view and said: If it were so, then *Īlāf* would be part of the sūrah *Alam tara*. The consensus of all on separating the two shows that it indicates something other than what he said. He means al-Akhfash, al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ. (They said:) The phrase is related to the verb *ʿajibū* (wonder), understood, meaning: *"Wonder at the covenant of Quraysh, the caravan of winter and summer, and their abandoning the worship of the Lord of this House."* Then He commanded them to worship after that, and informed them that God is the One who fed them and secured them, not their own efforts. That is: *"let them worship the One who fed them through the prayer of their father,"* where He said: ﴿And provide them with fruits﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 37], *"and who secured them through his prayer,"* where he said: ﴿My Lord, make this land secure﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 35]. *"And do not occupy yourselves with journeys, which are only the pursuit of gain and the display of worldly things."*

Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad said: It is related to His saying: ﴿let them worship﴾, and the meaning is: *"Because God did this to Quraysh, and enabled them to enjoy this blessing, ﴿let them worship﴾"* – He commanded them to worship Him on account of their covenant of the journey. Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you ask, why did the *fāʾ* (then) enter? I say: Because of the conditional sense in the speech. The meaning is: *"If they do not do it, then let them worship Him for this..."*, in the sense that God's blessings upon them cannot be counted; if they do not worship Him for all His blessings, then let them worship Him for this one blessing, which is a manifest blessing. End.

The majority read ﴿*ītlāfi*﴾ (covenant) as the verbal noun of *ālafa* (Form IV). Ibn ʿĀmir read *līlāf* on the pattern *fiʿāl*, the verbal noun of *alifa* (Form I). One says: *alifa al-rajulu al-amra ilfan wa-ilāfan* (the man became accustomed to the matter), and *ālafahu ghayruhu iyyāhu īlāfan* (another made him accustomed to it). *Ālafa* may also come transitive with one object, like *alifa*. The poet said:

*"Of the sand-dwellers (al-mu'allafāt) a free white she-camel, the rays of the morning shining across her back."*

The seven readers did not differ in reading *ītlāfihim* as the verbal noun of the quadriliteral form. It is transmitted from Abū Bakr, from ʿĀṣim, that he read with two hamzas, the second being quiescent, and this is anomalous. Although the original form is so, they substituted the hamza which is the first radical of the word because of the heaviness of two hamzas together. They did not substitute in forms such as *yu'allafu* where it is obligatory, because the heaviness is removed by deleting the hamza in it. This narration from ʿĀṣim is through al-Shammanī, from al-Aʿshā, from Abū Bakr. Muḥammad ibn Dāwūd al-Naqqār narrated from ʿĀṣim: *"ʾiʾlāfihim"* with two hamzas, both kasrah, and after them a quiescent yā' arising from the vowel of the second hamza, when its kasrah was prolonged. The correct view is that ʿĀṣim retracted from the second hamza, and that he read like the group. Abū Jaʿfar, as al-Zamakhsharī related, read *li-ilfi Quraysh*. And he read, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya related, *ilfahum*. The poet said:

*"You claim that your brothers Quraysh have ilf (habit), and you have no ilāf (covenant)."*

He combined the two verbal nouns of the triliteral *alifa*. From Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn ʿĀmir: *ilāfahum* on the pattern *fiʿāl*. From Abū Jaʿfar and Ibn Kathīr: *ilfahum* on the pattern *fiʿl*, and with this ʿIkrimah read. Also from Abū Jaʿfar: *līlāf* with a quiescent yā' after the lām. He followed (the pattern) since he changed the second into a yā', and he deleted the first, a deletion without analogy. From ʿIkrimah: *li-yaʾlafa Quraysh* (that Quraysh may become accustomed), and from him also: *li-taʾlaf Quraysh* in the imperative form. From him and from Hilāl ibn Fityān: with a fatḥah on the lām of the imperative.

They all agreed here on the *ṣarf* (declension) of Quraysh, taking into account the meaning of a living group. It is permissible not to decline it, considering the meaning of tribe, because of feminine gender and proper-name status. The poet said:

*"And Quraysh sufficed for the difficult matters and led them."*

Sibawayh treated it as a name for a tribe, as in *Maʿadd*, *Quraysh* and *Thaqīf*. The use of this for living groups is more common, but if you make it a name for tribes, it is permissible and good.

The majority read ﴿*riḥlata*﴾ with a kasrah on the rāʾ. Abū al-Simmāl read it with a ḍammah. With the kasrah it is a verbal noun; with the ḍammah it is the direction to which one travels. The majority hold that they are two journeys: one to Syria for trade and gaining profit, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"Two journeys between them for him and for others, the journey of winter and the caravans of summer."*

Ibn ʿAbbās said: One journey is to Yemen, and one journey to Buṣrā. He also said: They travel in summer to al-Ṭāʾif, where there is water and shade, and they travel in winter to Makkah for trade and their other purposes. Al-Zamakhsharī said: He meant the two journeys of winter and summer, and used the singular to avoid confusion, like his saying:

*"Eat in the part of your belly so that you may be chaste, for your time is a lean time."*

End. According to Sibawayh, this is not permissible except in poetic necessity. Similar is the line:

*"O dove of the belly of the two valleys, sing!"*

He meant *"the two bellies of the two valleys"*. Our companions cited it as poetic necessity. Al-Naḥḥās said: They had four journeys. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: This view is rejected. End. It should not be objected to, since the people of the *īlāf* were four brothers, the sons of ʿAbd Manāf: Hāshim, who made a covenant with the king of Syria and took horses from him, so he was secure in his trade to Syria; ʿAbd Shams, who made a covenant with Abyssinia; al-Muṭṭalib, to Yemen; and Nawfal, to Persia. These were called *al-mujbirūn* (the ones who restrain), so the caravans of Quraysh travelled to the cities under the protection of these brothers, and they were not attacked.

Al-Azharī said: *Īlāf* resembles a guarantee of protection for a fee. If that is so, then it is permissible that they had four journeys, according to these places in which the merchants were under the protection of these four. Concerning them the poet praised them:

*"O man who changes his saddle, why not dismount among the family of ʿAbd Manāf?*
*Those who take the covenant from its horizons, and who travel for the journey of the covenant (īlāf).*
*Those who give shelter, though no one is given shelter by them, and who say: 'Come, for the guests!'*
*And who mix their rich with their poor, until their poor becomes like the stone (al-kāf)."*

So ﴿*riḥlata*﴾ here is a collective noun that can apply to one or to more. Their *ītlāf* is an appositive (*badal*) of ﴿the covenant of Quraysh﴾. He left the substituted term unrestricted and restricted the substitute with the direct object, which is *riḥla*, meaning: *"because they became accustomed to a journey,"* magnifying the matter of the covenant and reminding of the great blessing in it.

﴿this House﴾ is the Kaʿbah. This expression became firmly established here because of the earlier mention of its protection in the previous sūrah. *Min* here indicates cause, meaning *"because of hunger"*. They were settled people in a land without crops, exposed to hunger and fear, were it not for God's gentle care for them, and this was through the prayer of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him. God says: ﴿To it are brought the fruits of every thing﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 57].

﴿who fed them against﴾ He favoured them over the Arabs in that they were secure wherever they alighted; it was said: These are the inhabitants of God's House, so no one would touch them, while others were in fear.

Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: ﴿who fed them against﴾ means against leprosy, so you do not see a leper in Makkah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: The indefiniteness in *ḥunger* and *fear* is for their severity; meaning: He fed them through the two journeys from a severe hunger they were in before them, and secured them from a great fear, namely the fear of the People of the Elephant, or the fear of being snatched away in their land and in their travels. The majority read ﴿*min khawf*﴾ with the *nūn* clearly pronounced before the *khāʾ*. Al-Musayyabī, from Nāfiʿ, read it with the *nūn* concealed (*ikhfāʾ*), and similarly before the ʿayn, as in *min ʿalā*. This is a dialect related by Sibawayh. Ibn al-Aslat addressed Quraysh:

*"So rise, and pray to your Lord, and wipe yourselves against the corners of this House between the two mountains.*
*For you there is from it a trial and a witness, on the day of Abū Makāsim, guide of the battalions.*
*A sandy mound in the plain moving, and a journey upon the swift camels on the heads of the cliffs.*
*When the victory of the Lord of the Throne came to you, the soldiers of the King turned them back between leg and sabre.*
*So they fled hastily in flight, and none returned to their family except the scattered remnants."*

This expression became firmly established here because of the earlier mention of its protection in the previous sūrah. *Min* here indicates cause, meaning *"because of hunger"*. They were settled people in a land without crops, exposed to hunger and fear, were it not for God's gentle care for them, and this was through the prayer of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon him. God says: ﴿To it are brought the fruits of every thing﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 57].

﴿who fed them against﴾ He favoured them over the Arabs in that they were secure wherever they alighted; it was said: These are the inhabitants of God's House, so no one would touch them, while others were in fear.

Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: ﴿who fed them against﴾ means against leprosy, so you do not see a leper in Makkah. Al-Zamakhsharī said: The indefiniteness in *ḥunger* and *fear* is for their severity; meaning: He fed them through the two journeys from a severe hunger they were in before them, and secured them from a great fear, namely the fear of the People of the Elephant, or the fear of being snatched away in their land and in their travels. The majority read ﴿*min khawf*﴾ with the *nūn* clearly pronounced before the *khāʾ*. Al-Musayyabī, from Nāfiʿ, read it with the *nūn* concealed (*ikhfāʾ*), and similarly before the ʿayn, as in *min ʿalā*. This is a dialect related by Sibawayh. Ibn al-Aslat addressed Quraysh:

*"So rise, and pray to your Lord, and wipe yourselves against the corners of this House between the two mountains.*
*For you there is from it a trial and a witness, on the day of Abū Makāsim, guide of the battalions.*
*A sandy mound in the plain moving, and a journey upon the swift camels on the heads of the cliffs.*
*When the victory of the Lord of the Throne came to you, the soldiers of the King turned them back between leg and sabre.*
*So they fled hastily in flight, and none returned to their family except the scattered remnants."*
